key_insight: Pretrained protein language models (pLMs) can leak information from training data into downstream protein–protein interaction (PPI) inference models, causing artificially inflated performance metrics. This means reported gains may reflect data leakage rather than true predictive power.
problem_solved: Identifies and documents a source of hidden data leakage in PPI inference workflows that undermines reliable evaluation of models using pretrained pLM embeddings.
method: Systematic evaluation of PPI inference models that use pLM embeddings to detect when pretrained knowledge boosts apparent performance.
Controlled experiments comparing model performance with and without pretraining-derived signals or with stricter train/test splits to quantify inflation from leakage.
Analysis of how overlap between sequences seen during pLM pretraining and downstream evaluation can produce misleading results and proposed evaluation controls.
impact: Alerts AI/ML practitioners and bioinformaticians that using off‑the‑shelf pLM embeddings can introduce subtle data leakage, so benchmarks and model choices must be adjusted to ensure valid PPI evaluation. Encourages adoption of stricter splitting strategies and leakage-aware baselines.
visual_elements: Flow diagram showing pipeline: pLM pretraining → embedding extraction → PPI model → evaluation, with a highlighted leakage path from pretraining to evaluation.
Bar chart comparing PPI performance scores with 'standard' vs 'leakage-controlled' evaluation to show score inflation.
Dataset split schematic (train/validation/test) illustrating safe vs unsafe splitting (sequence overlap vs no-overlap).
Icon set: protein chains, model/embedding vector, warning/exclamation to signal leakage risk.
paper_title: A flaw in using pretrained protein language models in protein–protein interaction inference models
